en: The men to read the Quran
He had now made ready;
Wearing them down, beating and marching them under guard,
He had driven them here.
Setting up a dwelling in Talas,
From those mighty men who came to see him,
Hiding Sultan Manas,
That formidable woman Kanykei,
Her splendid hair as thick as a girth,
Had bound tight upon her crown.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
With her son left young behind him
And all his brothers hostile,
Was governing the people then.
Her many sorrows overflowed her heart;
Your fierce sister-in-law Kanykei,
Her tears streaming in ten directions,
Her thoughts cruelly torn apart,
Her tears pouring down:
“God will take the generous one,” she thought.
“That dear lion, greater than the world,
May be left without a memorial,” she thought.
She had six hundred pack camels saddled,
Had their ropes set firmly right;
Beyond Andijan,
Across from Namangan,
Within the reach of the khan of Kokand,
The earth of fire-resistant clay
She had brought by hired transport.
She had it mixed in a great vat,
Had goat hair sprinkled in,
Had cattle hair added;
Aksakal’s son,
The mighty Sart Aralbay,
And sixty strong men wielding hoes
She had tread that clay.
“Give six thousand wether goats,” she said,
Laying a levy on the Argyn.
Giving not a stone, let alone a wether goat,
The Argyn moved away.
“Give seven thousand wether goats,” she said,
Laying a levy on the Kyrgyz.
Giving not shit, let alone a wether goat,
The Kyrgyz moved away.
When the Kyrgyz would not submit,
It was as though, when their khan died, they too had died—
Those bastards had been left thus,
All that great people dead!
Or were they a people short of wether goats?
Your noble Manas, the leopard—
Was he a lion for whom they should begrudge them?
Unable to find a way, crying out,
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykei
Stood there weeping bitterly.
(What is seen today is gone tomorrow—
Alas, such is this wayward world.)
Making their knees bend to the earth,
Your champion Koyonaaly
Drove them into Talas,
The forty holy men running.
Dust rose where he went;
That impish Koyonaaly—
When they heard his fame from afar,
The Argyn people were scared out of their wits.
They yielded to what was demanded, they say;
The wether goats levied upon them
The Argyn drove in, they say.
They accepted the levy, they say;
Through fear of that young man,
The Kyrgyz drove theirs in, they say.
That dear woman Kanykei
She slaughtered seven thousand wether goats,
Fired bricks and built it strong:
“For seven centuries to come,
My perfect champion’s mausoleum
Must stand unbroken,” she said, and built.
She slaughtered six thousand wether goats,
Fired bricks and built it strong:
“For six centuries to come,
My generous one’s mausoleum
Must stand unbroken,” she said, and built.
Supkojo of broad Mecca—
She had Supkojo brought.
She had fanciful designs carved inside;
The stories left by Manas
She had shown in great pictures.
“When he grows, the orphan will come,” she thought.
“The courage of his father,
If he survives, the child will know.
‘My father was Manas,’
The child will know at last.
What his disgraced mother did,
My foal will know, unless he is a fool.”
At the entrance of the mausoleum,
Bakybai and Duulat, the two khans,
He portrayed them in a picture.
Khan Alooko and Azizkhan—
He portrayed them in a picture.
The haze that hung over Beijing,
The road he portrayed in a picture.
The great host that bore such hardship—
The host he portrayed in a picture.
He showed him mounted on Akkula,
Clothed in the white armored coat,
With Zulpuqor, descended from the sky,
Fastened snugly to his wrist,
Upon the swarming dark unbelievers
Charging and wreaking slaughter,
The unbelievers farther off
Felling with his spear.
The mottled gray pennant and red banner
He put in Khan Bakai’s hand,
Making the Chinese cry out,
Toward Khan Manas, the leopard,
He showed them driven in the picture.
Clothed in a coat of blue ribbed cloth,
Mounted on a horse like Kogala,
Tall in stature, broad of shoulder,
Akbaltai’s son Chubak,
Wreaking slaughter on the Chinese;
Joloy of the Kalmyks
He showed Khan Chubak spearing—
Him he portrayed in a picture.
On one side of that,
Mounted on a horse like Kokchebich,
Its long-haired tail tied in a tight knot,
Ruddy of complexion, radiant of face,
With a leather belt about his waist,
If seven myriads of dark troops came,
He would charge them with his coat thrown open,
Never turning back without drinking blood,
Never shrinking from death.
Yesterday, upon imperial Beijing,
When he advanced, besieging and driving them,
Making the Chinese cry aloud,
When he beat and drove them on,
Breaking ranks in spear combat,
At the age of twenty-one
His allotted death came, and he fell to a shot.
Khan Ulak’s son Syrgak,
Khan Manas’s impish champion—
Him he portrayed in a picture.
Mounted on dear Sarala,
Wearing a golden belt,
His moonlike face lit with radiance,
Wearing a silver belt,
His sunlike face lit with radiance;
Yesterday he had yellow willows planted,
His willows remained in Beijing.
Made of yellow gold,
His throne remained in Beijing.
He had stained his golden throne with blood:
“He will not enter the present faith,” he said,
And slew his father Azizkhan.
He had bloodied his silver throne:
“His sin is too great,” he said,
And slew his elder brother Kun Zhang-Zhung.
Purified of the dark faith,
He fled the unbelievers and became a stranger.
With a golden forelock and tasseled sash,
Azizkhan’s only son—
Him he portrayed in a picture.
Old Kyrgyl, leader of the forty,
Khan Shuutu of good disposition—
The men he portrayed in a picture.
Then that poor woman Kanykei,
Without a single soul knowing,
Without a single person seeing,
From the lands of Zhelpinish and Urum
Had seventy mighty men brought.
“My noble, clear-sighted leader,
They will open his grave and take him,” she thought.
“They will drag him upon the road
And have the dogs tear him apart.
The crooked-hearted enemies
Will take their revenge this way,” she thought.
At Echkilik’s black cliff,
That immense and towering mountain,
She supplied iron crowbars,
And sharp steel hoes;
She had the face of the cliff opened,
Had Manas’s resting place dug,
Had its entrance fashioned
Wide enough for a single person,
And the farther part hollowed out
To hold six thousand sheep.
“Lest its roof fall in,” she thought,
In eighty places around it
She set up gilded pillars.
“Let the inside lie bright,” she thought;
She had ruby stones split
And in eighty places
Had them set as lamps.
“Lest the inside rot,” she thought;
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
Showing her lion’s courage,
Had a way broken through with iron crowbars,
Showing her skill,
The dark spring water flowing above
She had led through the interior.
She had a golden couch built,
And covered it with fine white cloth.
“Lest the underside rot,” she thought,
She had juniper ashes spread.
Without letting one person know,
Without letting a single soul suspect,
Without showing the six villains,
Without making it known to the people,
She tended Manas.
If anyone knew a hint of it,
Your sister-in-law deceived and killed them.
For Manas lying ill,
She carefully prepared his belongings;
The dead warrior had not the smallest regret left.
Then fierce Kanykei
Joined what had been broken,
Gathered what had been scattered,
And did not cease her tears.
Precious coins of yellow gold
She gathered for his funeral.
The Muslims of the Islamic faith
Wept in sorrow.
The reason for their weeping:
The leopard was the pillar of the faith.
When they girded themselves, that dear lion—
Was not Manas their backbone?
When they met a task in dire distress,
Without leaving them in ruin,
Was it not Manas who cared for them?
Leaving no part of the earth untouched,
Was it not Manas who ranged across it?
His wrath struck terror into souls;
At the head of the mighty people,
Was it not Manas who stood?
The Chinese upon the ridges—
Was it not Manas who slew them?
All that he did before Allah—
Was it not Manas who won His favor?
The Argyn and the Kyrgyz,
Letting no wind break through from any side,
Was it not Manas who sheltered them?
His fortune was complete;
His heart was a boundless river and lake.
He was a lion upheld by his patron saint.
Yielding to none in all the world,
The lion Manas was a hero.
A grievous sickness came upon him;
Your fierce wolf put them through such trials.
His whiskered mustache drooping,
Setting out toward Judgment Day,
Now his illness grew severe.
As Manas lay upon his pillow,
And fierce Kanykei bore the hardship alone,
She sent word to the khan.
A day of terrible trouble came
For all the people.
